extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in literature and literary controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing memoir-style novels (especially disputed/hoax memoirs) with attention to authorial authenticity, cultural representation, narrative craft, historical context, and reception. Focuses on how provenance and author background affect interpretation and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical authenticity / truthfulness of authorial claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the work accurately promoted as an autobiography or is it a fictionalized account/hoax? (The Education of Little Tree "was promoted as an authentic autobiography... [but] the book was proven to be a literary hoax... based on Carter's fanciful and fraudulent family claims.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check provenance and external documentation identifying the real author (e.g., exposés, archival research). Consider publisher statements and later reclassification. A demonstrated hoax changes interpretive framing and raises ethical questions; reviewers should note when a claimed memoir is actually fictionalized or fraudulent. Example anti-pattern: accepting publisher blurbs or author pseudonyms at face value without independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate cultural representation of Indigenous (Cherokee) language and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the text accurately represent Cherokee words, customs, and cultural practices? ("Members of the Cherokee Nation have said that so-called 'Cherokee' words and many customs in The Education of Little Tree are inaccurate, and they point out that the novel's characters are stereotyped.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity to source community knowledge and consult community voices or scholarship. Stereotyping or invented 'native' elements reduce authenticity and can cause harm. Consider input from the represented community; cultural inaccuracy is a substantive defect in ethnographic or claimed-autobiographical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's personal/political background and its ethical impact on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the author's known biography (e.g., prior political activism, affiliations) affect reading and evaluation? (Carter "had been an active participant in several white supremacist organizations, including the Ku Klux Klan...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor the author's past actions and public positions into assessments of moral authority, possible hypocrisy, and the ethical context of themes. Consider documented links between the author's prior rhetoric/affiliations and themes in the work. Example: high-profile revelations about the author led to re-evaluation and removal of endorsements (Oprah pulled the book from recommended titles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification and publisher labeling (fiction vs. memoir)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the work correctly classified and marketed (memoir/autobiography vs fiction)? ("When Carter's background was widely publicized in 1991, the book was reclassified by the publisher as fiction.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the publisher and marketing accurately reflect the book's nature. Misclassification misleads readers and affects critical interpretation; correct labeling is a publishing-ethics criterion. Reviewers should note any reclassifications and their justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative themes, voice, and stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the central themes and stylistic choices (environmentalism, simple living, mystical Native American theme, devices such as repeated phrasing)? (The book attracted readers with its message of environmentalism and simple living and frequently uses devices like ending paragraphs with short statements beginning 'Which'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how themes are rendered and whether stylistic devices (repetition, pacing) support the work's aims. Note structural choices — e.g., the article observes that toward the end "the book's pace speeds up dramatically and its detail decreases." Evaluate whether such choices enhance or weaken the narrative. Consider coming-of-age arc, voice authenticity, and consistency of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of historical context and social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the book accurately and sensitively depict historical settings and institutions (Prohibition, residential schools, prejudice of caretakers)? (Synopsis mentions Prohibition, a residential school, and prejudice toward Indians and the natural world.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify representations of historical institutions and their dynamics; assess whether portrayals are nuanced or reinforce stereotypes. For works set in specific historical contexts, factual grounding and sensitivity to trauma (e.g., residential schools) are important evaluative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception, commercial success, and institutional recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: How was the book received commercially and institutionally? (It "entered the New York Times Best Seller list and receiving the first American Booksellers Association Book of the Year (ABBY) award" and later had a film adaptation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record measurable reception: bestseller lists, awards, reissues, adaptations. These affect cultural impact but do not substitute for ethical or representational quality. Note when reception changes after revelations about authorship or background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly and public controversy as a lens for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the work a subject of scholarly scrutiny or public controversy (hoax, author's white supremacist background, documentaries, journalistic exposés)? (The book "has been the subject of a number of scholarly articles, many focusing on the hoax and on the impact of the author's white supremacist background on the work.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work generates controversy, include historiography and critical debates in evaluation. Consider documentary and journalistic treatments (e.g., This American Life episode, documentaries) as part of the reception history. Controversy can be an evaluative dimension in assessing cultural significance and ethical standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of authorial identity on interpretive meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author's revealed identity alter the perceived moral or thematic meaning of the work? ("a debate continues as to whether the book's lessons are altered by the identity of the author.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss whether reader responses and critical judgments change when the author's identity or past actions are known. Include divergent perspectives (e.g., Sherman Alexie's view that it may be 'an act of romantic atonement' versus seeing 'racial hypocrisy'). This criterion addresses whether text and author can be separated for evaluation.
